# Statement ledger

This ledger maps labels of the manuscript on the second moment of the
Stratonovich hyperbolic Anderson model with Gaussian noise fractional in time
to the Lean declarations in this package. Labels and TeX line numbers refer to
the manuscript revision a284420, and labels are written exactly as in its
LaTeX source (for example `P:clock-copy-obstruction`). The ledger was written
and reviewed at the earlier revisions cf979d6, 669ccc9, ba01d98, 3920258 and
975feb3. Revision a284420 makes two mathematical edits that the ledger
follows. (1) In `notes/integrated_spatial_occupation.tex` it adds Lemma
`L:spatial-fourier-bound` (lines 101-164, display `E:spatial-fourier-bound`),
the deterministic bound `A_sp(g) <= 2^(1+alpha) R_alpha b^(alpha/2)` that
`SpatialFourierBound` already proved, and the proof of
`P:spatial-smooth-ratio` (same label and statement) now derives `R_0 < inf`
from it, independently of the finiteness of `S_1^pos`, which it keeps only
for the score inequality. (2) In the main file, `L:damped-homogeneous-norms`
replaces its smoothing and truncation sentence by the multiplier comparison
`E:damped-multiplier-comparison` (a measurable multiplier `m` in `[0,1]`,
nested measurable Laplace domains, positivity after time integration,
scaling asserted only for the original covariance) and its proof by the
corresponding argument. The other changes since 975feb3 are prose and front
matter (title, abstract, preface, a theory-outlook chapter, the reader
edition, Appendices F and G, the list of notation moved to the back).
Every cited label exists exactly once at a284420. Three of them are new at
a284420 and do not exist at 975feb3: `L:spatial-fourier-bound`,
`E:spatial-fourier-bound` and `E:damped-multiplier-comparison`. Every other
cited label exists exactly once, in the same file, at both revisions, and
every such cited lemma, proposition, theorem, equation and section has the
same statement and proof up to whitespace and braces, except
`P:spatial-smooth-ratio` (proof only), `L:damped-homogeneous-norms`
(statement and proof) and the section `S:spatial-occupation-foundation`
(the new lemma). TeX line numbers were moved to a284420 by a line map; each
moved range has the same text at both revisions, and the ranges inside the
two edited passages were mapped to the corresponding new passages by hand
(script checks recorded in `provenance/manuscript-anchor.json`).

## Scope

- The "What it states" column is a faithful paraphrase, sometimes
  shortened. The exact statement is the Lean type in
  `StratonovichHAMAudit/<Module>.lean` (step modules) or
  `StratonovichHAMSecondMoment/<Module>.lean` (library modules: whole results, narrower results, foundations and proof steps);
  `Audit/<module>/` prints the elaborated types.
- The rows cover every public theorem (2050) and 418 definitions whose
  values are stated as facts or that name a manuscript object. The other 89
  public definitions have no rows of their own: 85 (for example `kappa`,
  `delta`, `gauge`, `counts`, `InventoryProduct.partialEval`,
  `OccupationPhysicalClass.volI`, `SpaceTimePositivity.timeMeasure`,
  `TerminalWick.chainMassReal`, `WaveGreenFourier.spherePhi` and
  `OccupationCeilingExact.stepG`) only name quantities or measures used in
  those statements, and four are the instances that make
  `TimeCompletion.Pre` a pre-inner-product space; read their bodies in the
  Lean source or in `Audit/`.
- The `StratonovichHAMAudit` modules check finite, algebraic and scalar
  steps only: exact identities, polynomial and rational certificates,
  real-power bookkeeping, parameter ranges, and a few finite-dimensional
  inner-product and finite-word facts. The exception is `HermiteWordFock`
  (wave L9), which applies `HermiteWord.cut_eq_raw` to the Fock model of
  `FockForm` and so formalizes the special case of `L:finite-word-cutoff`
  with one Gaussian coordinate per color (section "HermiteWordFock (narrower result: `L:finite-word-cutoff` for one Gaussian mode per color and single finite words; finite sums and Bochner integrals not formalized)"); the
  multi-mode case is not formalized.
- Section headings use three categories. (A) "whole result": every
  conclusion of the labelled result is a Lean conclusion under the
  manuscript's hypotheses, possibly with named supplied inputs that are
  disclosed (coverage class same-assumptions or inputs-supplied, conclusion
  full); no other section carries it. (B) "narrower result: ...": a labelled
  result some of whose conclusions are not Lean conclusions, or are proved
  for a modelled object (the class `O` by joint representatives, the rate in
  Rayleigh form, the cost in integral form, an abstract structure standing
  for an object the manuscript constructs, an object that is not constructed)
  whose identification with the manuscript's object is not formalized; the
  heading names what is missing. The one exception is a registered model
  choice (next item): a result whose only modelled object is such a choice
  stays a whole result, and its section names the model.
  Discharging a named input in a completion module does not turn a narrower
  result into a whole one. (C) "foundation: ..." or "proof steps ...": facts
  used by labelled results, not a labelled result themselves; every
  `StratonovichHAMAudit` section except `HermiteWordFock` is of this kind.
  The first cell of an Index row uses the same words.
- Model-choice register. A registered model choice is a documented
  definitional choice that is the standard construction of a manuscript
  object, recorded with the identification that is not formalized. M1 (wave
  L6, Le's decision 4): the wave Green measure in `d = 3` is
  `(s/(4 pi)) map (omega -> s omega) volume.toSphere`, Mathlib's sphere
  measure scaled to the radius-`s` sphere; its identification with the
  surface (Hausdorff or Riemannian) measure of the TeX is not proved. Results
  whose only modelled object is M1 (`L:low-alpha-convolution`,
  `L:phase-contractions`, and the sections `LowAlphaConvolution`,
  `PhaseContractions` and `L9Completed`) are whole results. Missing
  constructions are not model choices: they make a result narrower (for
  example the noise `W` of `P:masked-quotient-obstruction`, the ground

  `L:uniform-series-tail`, the operator paths of `P:radius-mean-anchor`, the
  solution moments of `P:moment-growth-logconvex` and

     3	## The paper's argument and where Lean enters
     4	
     5	The paper bounds and identifies the growth of `log E[u(t,x)²]` for the
     6	Stratonovich hyperbolic Anderson model. The argument has three layers.
     7	
     8	1. **Stochastic and analytic layer.** The chaos expansion, the two-chain
     9	   pairing integrals, Wick pairings (beyond finite families of Gaussian
    10	   values), Gaussian integration (beyond finitely many standard Gaussians),
    11	   imported bounds,
    12	   Laplace transforms and the variational asymptotics. **Not in Lean**,
    13	   except a few slices: the Laplace transforms of the wave kernel and of
    14	   the two-time kernel and the subordination formula (`ClockCopy` and its
    15	   foundation modules), the Gaussian transform of the spectral measure
    16	   (`MaskedSpectralGrowth`), the uniform scalar frequency row
    17	   (`FrequencyRow`), the temporal completion `H_a` (`TimeCompletion`), the
    18	   auxiliary mask norm (`MaskedAuxiliaryNorm`), the Gaussian heat envelope
    19	   of the covariance (`VariationalMean`), a finite Hilbert-valued Bessel
    20	   inequality (`PhaseBessel`), the wave Green measures `G_s` for
    21	   `d = 1, 2, 3` (`WaveGreen`), the spectral identity and positive
    22	   definiteness of `Gamma = delta_0(dx_1) dx_2` (`QuotientObstruction`), a
    23	   finite Gaussian comparison under the positive semidefinite order
    24	   (`GaussianComparison`), the two wave variance directions in spectral
    25	   form (`WaveTwoVariances`), the variational floor and the Rayleigh-form
    26	   rate (`VariationalFloor`, `VariationalRate`), the deterministic Fourier
    27	   bound `L:spatial-fourier-bound` for the smooth spatial ratio and the
    28	   static controls
    29	   (`SpatialFourierBound`, `SpatialSmoothRatio`, `SpatialStaticControls`,
    30	   `SpatialOccupationCompleted`), series types and the continuity of the
    31	   growth types in the temporal exponent (`SeriesType`, `TypeContinuity`),
    32	   the white-noise bound formulas and clock transforms
    33	   (`WhiteRelativeWidth`, `WhiteClockLaplace`), the coefficient bound of
    34	   the interval inventory product (`InventoryProduct`), an abstract `L^2`
    35	   limit of a regularized series under a uniform scaled moment bound
    36	   (`UniformSeriesTail`), the density of test functions in the
    37	   weak-gradient `H^1` (`H1Density`), the physical four-linear extension
    38	   and the spatial energy (`SpatialFourLinear`), the full physical
    39	   occupation class (`OccupationPhysicalClass`; both completed in
    40	   `SpatialOccupationL7Completed`), the scalar and Hilbert-space steps
    41	   of the static interaction and interval coefficient bounds
    42	   (`IntervalScalar`, `IntervalScalarCompleted`), the spectral-mass
    43	   identity `R_Gamma(1) = R_alpha` (`SpectralMassIdentity`), Gaussian
    44	   smoothing as a Fourier multiplier (`DampedMultiplier`), the positivity of
    45	   the space-time occupation form, the deterministic occupation ceiling and
    46	   the spatial bracket (`SpaceTimePositivity`, `OccupationCeilingFinite`,
    47	   `SpatialBracket`, completed in `L8Completed`), the masked rates
    48	   (`RemoveMask`), the finite Wick formula and the terminal-chain Wick
    49	   formula with the chain measures given by their masses (`FiniteWick`,
    50	   `TerminalWick`), an abstract compact Young baseline (`SymplecticFree`)
    51	   and the Cauchy steps of the static phase orders (`StaticPhaseCauchy`),
    52	   the Fourier transforms of the wave Green measures in `d = 1, 2, 3` and
    53	   Archimedes' law for the sphere measure (`WaveGreenFourier`), the low-alpha
    54	   convolution bound and the static contraction bounds
    55	   (`LowAlphaConvolution`, `PhaseContractions`, completed in `L9Completed`),
    56	   the exact occupation constant and ceiling (`RawOccupationEnergy`,
    57	   `OccupationCeilingExact`), the normalized Hermite polynomials and the
    58	   finite Gaussian Fock layer with values in a Hilbert factor
    59	   (`GaussianHermite`, `HermiteFock`) and their consumers `L:fock-form`,
    60	   `L:interval-contractions` and `E:occupied-multiplication` (`FockForm`),
    61	   and the scalar and numerical-range steps of the complex phase bounds
    62	   (`ComplexPhaseScalar`).
    63	2. **Reductions to explicit inequalities.** At many points the analytic
    64	   argument reduces to a finite statement: an exponent range, an exact
    65	   rational or square-root inequality, a polynomial that must stay positive
    66	   on a region, a determinant or matrix inverse, a count of coefficients in
    67	   a finite word, or an integral comparison once integrability is known.
    68	   **These are what Lean checks.**
    69	3. **Assembly** of the main theorems from the layers above. **Not in Lean.**
    70	
    71	So each module checks one reduction in layer 2. Its hypotheses state the
    72	facts that layer 1 supplies (for example positivity of a parameter,
    73	integrability of a function, or an inequality proved analytically in the
    74	paper). Its conclusion is the fact that the paper then uses.

     3	## The paper's argument and where Lean enters
     4	
     5	The paper bounds and identifies the growth of `log E[u(t,x)²]` for the
     6	Stratonovich hyperbolic Anderson model. The argument has three layers.
     7	
     8	1. **Stochastic and analytic layer.** The chaos expansion, the two-chain
     9	   pairing integrals, Wick pairings (beyond finite families of Gaussian
    10	   values), Gaussian integration (beyond finitely many standard Gaussians),
    11	   imported bounds,
    12	   Laplace transforms and the variational asymptotics. **Not in Lean**,
    13	   except a few slices: the Laplace transforms of the wave kernel and of
    14	   the two-time kernel and the subordination formula (`ClockCopy` and its
    15	   foundation modules), the Gaussian transform of the spectral measure
    16	   (`MaskedSpectralGrowth`), the uniform scalar frequency row
    17	   (`FrequencyRow`), the temporal completion `H_a` (`TimeCompletion`), the
    18	   auxiliary mask norm (`MaskedAuxiliaryNorm`), the Gaussian heat envelope
    19	   of the covariance (`VariationalMean`), a finite Hilbert-valued Bessel
    20	   inequality (`PhaseBessel`), the wave Green measures `G_s` for
    21	   `d = 1, 2, 3` (`WaveGreen`), the spectral identity and positive
    22	   definiteness of `Gamma = delta_0(dx_1) dx_2` (`QuotientObstruction`), a
    23	   finite Gaussian comparison under the positive semidefinite order
    24	   (`GaussianComparison`), the two wave variance directions in spectral
    25	   form (`WaveTwoVariances`), the variational floor and the Rayleigh-form
    26	   rate (`VariationalFloor`, `VariationalRate`), the deterministic Fourier
    27	   bound `L:spatial-fourier-bound` for the smooth spatial ratio and the
    28	   static controls
    29	   (`SpatialFourierBound`, `SpatialSmoothRatio`, `SpatialStaticControls`,
    30	   `SpatialOccupationCompleted`), series types and the continuity of the
    31	   growth types in the temporal exponent (`SeriesType`, `TypeContinuity`),
    32	   the white-noise bound formulas and clock transforms
    33	   (`WhiteRelativeWidth`, `WhiteClockLaplace`), the coefficient bound of
    34	   the interval inventory product (`InventoryProduct`), an abstract `L^2`
    35	   limit of a regularized series under a uniform scaled moment bound
    36	   (`UniformSeriesTail`), the density of test functions in the
    37	   weak-gradient `H^1` (`H1Density`), the physical four-linear extension
    38	   and the spatial energy (`SpatialFourLinear`), the full physical
    39	   occupation class (`OccupationPhysicalClass`; both completed in
    40	   `SpatialOccupationL7Completed`), the scalar and Hilbert-space steps
    41	   of the static interaction and interval coefficient bounds
    42	   (`IntervalScalar`, `IntervalScalarCompleted`), the spectral-mass
    43	   identity `R_Gamma(1) = R_alpha` (`SpectralMassIdentity`), Gaussian
    44	   smoothing as a Fourier multiplier (`DampedMultiplier`), the positivity of
    45	   the space-time occupation form, the deterministic occupation ceiling and
    46	   the spatial bracket (`SpaceTimePositivity`, `OccupationCeilingFinite`,
    47	   `SpatialBracket`, completed in `L8Completed`), the masked rates
    48	   (`RemoveMask`), the finite Wick formula and the terminal-chain Wick
    49	   formula with the chain measures given by their masses (`FiniteWick`,
    50	   `TerminalWick`), an abstract compact Young baseline (`SymplecticFree`)
    51	   and the Cauchy steps of the static phase orders (`StaticPhaseCauchy`),
    52	   the Fourier transforms of the wave Green measures in `d = 1, 2, 3` and
    53	   Archimedes' law for the sphere measure (`WaveGreenFourier`), the low-alpha
    54	   convolution bound and the static contraction bounds
    55	   (`LowAlphaConvolution`, `PhaseContractions`, completed in `L9Completed`),
    56	   the exact occupation constant and ceiling (`RawOccupationEnergy`,
    57	   `OccupationCeilingExact`), the normalized Hermite polynomials and the
    58	   finite Gaussian Fock layer with values in a Hilbert factor
    59	   (`GaussianHermite`, `HermiteFock`) and their consumers `L:fock-form`,
    60	   `L:interval-contractions` and `E:occupied-multiplication` (`FockForm`),
    61	   and the scalar and numerical-range steps of the complex phase bounds
    62	   (`ComplexPhaseScalar`).
    63	2. **Reductions to explicit inequalities.** At many points the analytic
    64	   argument reduces to a finite statement: an exponent range, an exact
    65	   rational or square-root inequality, a polynomial that must stay positive
    66	   on a region, a determinant or matrix inverse, a count of coefficients in
    67	   a finite word, or an integral comparison once integrability is known.
    68	   **These are what Lean checks.**
    69	3. **Assembly** of the main theorems from the layers above. **Not in Lean.**

    72	facts that layer 1 supplies (for example positivity of a parameter,
    73	integrability of a function, or an inequality proved analytically in the
    74	paper). Its conclusion is the fact that the paper then uses.

   105	result: ...": a labelled result some of whose conclusions are not Lean
   106	conclusions, or are proved for a modelled object (such as the class `O` by
   107	joint representatives, or the rate in Rayleigh form and the cost in integral
   108	form) whose identification with the manuscript's object is not formalized;
   109	the heading names what is missing. (C) "foundation: ..." or "proof steps of
   110	...": facts used by labelled results, not a labelled result themselves; the
   111	`StratonovichHAMAudit` step modules are all of this kind.

   114	pieces of other results is counted once. Completion modules

   135	## Reading a statement
   136	
   137	For each declaration, check three things against the paper:
   138	
   139	1. the hypotheses match what the paper has available at that point;
   140	2. the conclusion is what the paper uses next;
   141	3. parameter ranges, strict versus non-strict inequalities and quantifier
   142	   order agree.

   144	The [statement ledger](docs/statement-ledger.md) records this for every row.
   145	`Audit/<module>/` prints the full elaborated types, so the statements can be
   146	read without opening an editor.

   102	inputs that are disclosed (coverage class same-assumptions or
   103	inputs-supplied, conclusion full; at present every whole result has the

   107	joint representatives, or the rate in Rayleigh form and the cost in integral
   108	form) whose identification with the manuscript's object is not formalized;
   109	the heading names what is missing. (C) "foundation: ..." or "proof steps of
   110	...": facts used by labelled results, not a labelled result themselves; the
   111	`StratonovichHAMAudit` step modules are all of this kind.

  760| \begin{remark}[Source fidelity]\label{R:source-uniformity}
  761|   The author version's Remark~5.1 refers to (4.4), but (4.4), on p.~22, is a
  762|   smoothing limit. The relevant bound is (5.4), on p.~35, $\E X_n(t,x)^2 \le
  763|   C^nt^{2n}/n!$, with the preceding sentence asserting that $C$ is independent
  764|   of $n$ and $t$. Taken for all $t > 0$, this uniformity
  765|   contradicts~\eqref{E:white-test} at $n = 1$. The proof on pp.~34--35 sets
  766|   $\theta = n/t$. Its first-norm estimate uses (A.1), which is finite for every
  767|   positive $\theta$ but does not give a constant uniform as $\theta\downarrow0$.
  768|   Its second-norm estimate uses the large-$\theta$ bound (A.3) without retaining
  769|   that restriction. Both losses of uniformity matter when $n/t$ is small. This
  770|   is a source-internal uniformity discrepancy; it does not refute Remark~5.1's
  771|   final large-time conclusion. The next lemma repairs this particular deduction
  772|   without importing the asserted uniformity of (5.4).
  773| \end{remark}

  803| \begin{lemma}[Homogeneous damped norms and temporal tails]
  804|   \label{L:damped-homogeneous-norms}
  805|   Under Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, the integrals
  806|   in~\eqref{E:damped-norm-definitions} are finite for every $\theta > 0$, with
  807|   $N_2(\theta)^2 \ge 0$, and
  808|   \[
  809|     N_0(\theta)=\theta^{-2},\qquad
  810|     N_1(\theta)=\theta^{\alpha+\alpha_0-2}N_1(1),\qquad
  811|     N_2(\theta)^2=\theta^{-\beta}N_2(1)^2,
  812|     \quad\beta=4-\alpha-\alpha_0.
  813|   \]
  814|   Let
  815|   \[
  816|     K_M(r)=\frac1{\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(\alpha_0)}
  817|     \int_M^\infty e^{-\lambda|r|}\lambda^{\alpha_0-1}\ud\lambda.
  818|   \]
  819|   Denote by $N_1^{(M)}(1)$ the first norm with $\lambda > M$, and by
  820|   $N_2^{(M)}(1)$ the second norm with $K_M(s-t)$ in place of
  821|   $|s-t|^{-\alpha_0}$. Then
  822|   \begin{equation}\label{E:damped-tail-norms}
  823|     N_1^{(M)}(1)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
  824|     N_2^{(M)}(1)\longrightarrow0\quad(M\to\infty).
  825|   \end{equation}
  826|   More precisely, let $m:\R^d\to[0,1]$ be measurable and let
  827|   $S\subset S'\subset(0,\infty)$ be measurable. Define $N_{1,m,S}(\theta)$
  828|   by replacing $\mu$ with $m\mu$ and restricting the $\lambda$ integral in
  829|   $N_1$ to $S$. Define $N_{2,m,S}(\theta)^2$ by replacing $\mu$ with $m\mu$
  830|   and the temporal kernel in $N_2^2$ with
  831|   \[
  832|     K_S(r)=\frac1{\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(\alpha_0)}
  833|     \int_S e^{-\lambda|r|}\lambda^{\alpha_0-1}\ud\lambda.
  834|   \]
  835|   Then, for every $\theta>0$,

  141| \begin{lemma}[Temporal covariance completion]\label{L:masked-time-completion}
  142|   Let $T > 0$. The form
  143|   \[
  144|     \langle f,g\rangle_a
  145|     = \int_0^T\int_0^T f(t)g(s)|t-s|^{-a}\ud t\ud s
  146|   \]
  147|   is positive semidefinite on real compact smooth tests. Its null-quotient
  148|   completion $H_a$ is separable. The inclusion of tests extends continuously
  149|   from $L^2(0,T)$, with

  154|   $f(t)\overline{f(s)}$. In particular, bounded measurable amplitudes on a
  155|   subinterval, extended by zero, belong to this completion.

1	\section{Finite Gaussian moments and whole-space Sobolev compactness}
     2	\label{S:compact-gaussian}
     3	
     4	We prove the finite Gaussian and compact-cutoff estimates needed to construct
     5	the wave operator path. All traces and Schatten norms in this section are
     6	unnormalized. The spatial states remain on $\R^d$, $d \in \{1,2,3\}$. Here $p$
     7	is an auxiliary Schatten and Gaussian-moment index. The auxiliary periodic space
     8	below is used only to factor a compactly supported multiplication operator. No
     9	infinite Gaussian series or time path is constructed in this section.
    10	
    11	\subsection{Finite Gaussian matrices with both variance powers}
    12	
    13	\begin{lemma}[Scalar power estimates]\label{L:gaussian-scalar-powers}
    14	  For $0 < \theta < 1$ and $u,v \ge 0$,
    15	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-weighted-power}
    16	    u^\theta v^{1-\theta} \le \theta u+(1-\theta)v.
    17	  \end{equation}
    18	  Consequently, if $L > 0$ and $0 \le q \le L$ are integers, then for real
    19	  $x,y$,
    20	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-integer-power}
    21	    |x|^q|y|^{L-q}
    22	    \le \frac qL|x|^L+\frac{L-q}L|y|^L.
    23	  \end{equation}
    24	  For nonnegative finite sequences, the usual H\"older inequality holds with
    25	  exponents $m$ and $m/(m-1)$, $m > 1$. If $Z \ge 0$ has finite expectation $F$
    26	  and $0 < r < 1$, then $\E Z^r \le F^r$.
    27	\end{lemma}
    28	
    29	\begin{proof}
    30	  If $v > 0$, divide~\eqref{E:gaussian-weighted-power} by $v$ and put $t = u/v$.
    31	  The function $\theta t+1-\theta-t^\theta$ decreases to zero at one and then
    32	  increases, by its derivative $\theta(1-t^{\theta-1})$. Continuity covers $t =
    33	  0$; if $v = 0$ the inequality is immediate. For $0 < q < L$, apply this with
    34	  $u = |x|^L$, $v = |y|^L$ and $\theta = q/L$. The endpoint cases $q = 0,L$ are
    35	  identities, with the ordinary integer convention $a^0 = 1$.
    36	
    37	  To prove finite H\"older, divide the two sequences by their respective
    38	  $\ell^m$ and $\ell^{m/(m-1)}$ norms. If either norm vanishes, the result is
    39	  immediate. Apply~\eqref{E:gaussian-weighted-power} with $\theta = 1/m$ to the
    40	  corresponding normalized powers and sum; the sum of products is at most one.
    41	  Undo the normalization. Finally, $F = 0$ gives $Z = 0$ almost surely. If $F >
    42	  0$, apply \eqref{E:gaussian-weighted-power} to $u = Z/F$, $v = 1$ and $\theta
    43	  = r$, and integrate. The right side has expectation one. This proves
    44	  Lemma~\ref{L:gaussian-scalar-powers}.
    45	\end{proof}
    46	
    47	\begin{lemma}[Two Hermitian trace bounds]\label{L:gaussian-trace-bounds}
    48	  Let $B,Y$ be finite Hermitian matrices, $m \ge 2$ an integer, and $L = 2m-2$.
    49	  For integers $0 \le q \le L$,
    50	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-trace-word}
    51	    \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(BY^qBY^{L-q})
    52	    \le \operatorname{Tr}(B^2|Y|^L).
    53	  \end{equation}
    54	  If $D \ge 0$ is Hermitian, then
    55	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-trace-holder}
    56	    \operatorname{Tr}(D|Y|^{2m-2})
    57	    \le (\operatorname{Tr}D^m)^{1/m}
    58	    (\operatorname{Tr}|Y|^{2m})^{(m-1)/m}.
    59	  \end{equation}
    60	\end{lemma}
    61	
    62	\begin{proof}
    63	  Diagonalize $Y$, with real eigenvalues $\lambda_i$, and write $b_{ij}$ for the
    64	  entries of $B$ in that basis. Hermitian symmetry gives $b_{ji} =
    65	  \overline{b_{ij}}$. The trace word is the real sum
    66	  \[
    67	    \sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2\lambda_j^q\lambda_i^{L-q}.
    68	  \]
    69	  Bound each product by its absolute value and use
    70	  \eqref{E:gaussian-integer-power}. After interchanging $i,j$, the two resulting
    71	  sums agree because $|b_{ij}| = |b_{ji}|$. Each equals
    72	  $\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2|\lambda_i|^L = \operatorname{Tr}(B^2|Y|^L)$. The two
    73	  weights sum to one, proving \eqref{E:gaussian-trace-word}. No commutation of
    74	  $B$ and $Y$ is used.
    75	
    76	  In the same basis put $d_i = D_{ii} \ge 0$. If $\theta_j$ are the nonnegative
    77	  eigenvalues of $D$, a unitary change of basis gives $d_i =
    78	  \sum_j|U_{ij}|^2\theta_j$. Both row and column sums of $|U_{ij}|^2$ equal one.
    79	  Finite convexity therefore yields
    80	  \[
    81	    \sum_i d_i^m \le \sum_{i,j}|U_{ij}|^2\theta_j^m
    82	    = \operatorname{Tr}D^m.
    83	  \]
    84	  For completeness, the convexity step follows from $t^m \ge s^m+ms^{m-1}(t-s)$
    85	  for $s,t \ge 0$, obtained by differentiating the difference. Average this
    86	  inequality with $s$ equal to the weighted mean. Now apply finite H\"older from
    87	  Lemma~\ref{L:gaussian-scalar-powers} to $\sum_i d_i|\lambda_i|^{2m-2}$. Since
    88	  $(2m-2)m/(m-1) = 2m$, the last display proves \eqref{E:gaussian-trace-holder},
    89	  including zero sums. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:gaussian-trace-bounds}.
    90	\end{proof}
    91	
    92	The estimate below is a finite-dimensional Gaussian noncommutative Khintchine
    93	inequality. For its origins in the work of Lust-Piquard and a Gaussian
    94	integration-by-parts proof, see Tropp~\cite{tropp:source2018:second-order}*{arXiv:1504.05919v2,
    95	Proposition~2.3 and Section~7}. We include the proof and Hermitian dilation
    96	to fix the normalization and retain both variance operators.
    97	
    98	\begin{proposition}[Finite Gaussian matrix moment]\label{P:finite-gaussian-matrix}
    99	  Let $A_1,\ldots,A_N$ be complex $o$-by-$n$ matrices, with $o,n,N \ge 1$, and
   100	  let $g_k$ be independent real standard Gaussians. Put
   101	  \[
   102	    X=\sum_k g_kA_k,\qquad V_{\rm out}=\sum_k A_kA_k^*,
   103	    \qquad V_{\rm in}=\sum_k A_k^*A_k.
   104	  \]
   105	  For even $p = 2m \ge 2$, with $\|A\|_{S_p}^p = \operatorname{Tr}((A^*A)^m)$,
   106	  \begin{align}
   107	    (\E\|X\|_{S_p}^p)^{1/p}
   108	    &\le \sqrt{p-1}\left(
   109	    \frac{\operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm out}^m+
   110	    \operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm in}^m}{2}\right)^{1/p}
   111	    \label{E:finite-gaussian-average}\\
   112	    &\le \sqrt{p-1}\max\left(
   113	    \|V_{\rm out}^{1/2}\|_{S_p},\|V_{\rm in}^{1/2}\|_{S_p}\right).
   114	    \label{E:finite-gaussian-maximum}
   115	  \end{align}
   116	  The constants are independent of $o,n,N$. The first inequality is an equality
   117	  at $p = 2$. Empty or zero families give the zero identity.
   118	\end{proposition}
   119	
   120	\begin{proof}
   121	  First suppose $B_k$ are Hermitian and put $Y = \sum_k g_kB_k$ and $D = \sum_k
   122	  B_k^2$. All polynomial moments are finite because Gaussian decay dominates
   123	  every fixed power. Componentwise integration by parts against the product
   124	  Gaussian density gives $\E[g_kP(g)] = \E[\partial_kP(g)]$, with zero boundary
   125	  terms. It applies to complex polynomials through their real and imaginary
   126	  parts; absolute polynomial integrability justifies Fubini.
   127	
   128	  For $m \ge 2$, put $F = \E\operatorname{Tr}Y^{2m}$ and $L = 2m-2$. Write
   129	  $\operatorname{Tr}Y^{2m} = \sum_k g_k \operatorname{Tr}(B_kY^{2m-1})$ and
   130	  differentiate the $2m-1$ factors in their order. This gives exactly
   131	  \[
   132	    F=\sum_k\sum_{q=0}^{L}
   133	    \E\operatorname{Tr}(B_kY^qB_kY^{L-q}).
   134	  \]
   135	  The eigenbasis calculation above shows these traces are real. The
   136	  differentiated polynomial is real by conjugation and trace cyclicity. No
   137	  derivative of a spectral absolute value or measurable choice of an eigenbasis
   138	  is needed. The two trace bounds give
   139	  \begin{align*}
   140	    F&\le (2m-1)\E\operatorname{Tr}(D|Y|^{2m-2})\\
   141	    &\le (2m-1)(\operatorname{Tr}D^m)^{1/m}
   142	    \E(\operatorname{Tr}|Y|^{2m})^{(m-1)/m}\\
   143	    &\le (2m-1)(\operatorname{Tr}D^m)^{1/m}F^{(m-1)/m}.
   144	  \end{align*}
   145	  Here $\operatorname{Tr}|Y|^{2m} = \operatorname{Tr}Y^{2m}$, and the last
   146	  inequality is the expectation bound in Lemma~\ref{L:gaussian-scalar-powers}.
   147	  If $F = 0$ the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise divide by its positive
   148	  fractional power and raise to $m$ to obtain
   149	  \begin{equation}\label{E:finite-hermitian-gaussian}
   150	    \E\operatorname{Tr}Y^{2m} \le (2m-1)^m\operatorname{Tr}D^m.
   151	  \end{equation}
   152	  For $m = 1$, independence gives directly $\E\operatorname{Tr}Y^2 =
   153	  \sum_k\operatorname{Tr}B_k^2 = \operatorname{Tr}D$, proving the same formula
   154	  as equality.
   155	
   156	  For rectangular $A_k$, use the Hermitian dilation
   157	  \[
   158	    B_k=\begin{pmatrix}0&A_k\\A_k^*&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
   159	    Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&X\\X^*&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
   160	    D=\operatorname{diag}(V_{\rm out},V_{\rm in}).
   161	  \]
   162	  Finite entrywise summation proves $\operatorname{Tr}(UV) =
   163	  \operatorname{Tr}(VU)$ for compatible rectangular matrices. Since $(XX^*)^m =
   164	  X(X^*X)^{m-1}X^*$, it follows that
   165	  \[
   166	    \operatorname{Tr}Y^{2m}=2\operatorname{Tr}((X^*X)^m),\qquad
   167	    \operatorname{Tr}D^m=\operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm out}^m+
   168	    \operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm in}^m.
   169	  \]
   170	  Substitute in~\eqref{E:finite-hermitian-gaussian}, divide by two and take the
   171	  $p$th root. This proves~\eqref{E:finite-gaussian-average}. For positive $V$,
   172	  spectral diagonalization gives $\|V^{1/2}\|_{S_p}^p = \operatorname{Tr}V^m$,
   173	  and the average of two nonnegative numbers is bounded by their maximum. At $p
   174	  = 2$, $\E\operatorname{Tr}X^*X = \operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm in} =
   175	  \operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm out}$, proving the claimed equality. This proves
   176	  Proposition~\ref{P:finite-gaussian-matrix}.
   177	\end{proof}
   178	
   179	\begin{remark}[Both variance directions are necessary]
   180	  \label{R:gaussian-one-variance-test}
   181	  Let $n = 16$ and $A_k = e_k^{\mathsf{T}}$ be the coordinate row matrices. The
   182	  only nonzero singular value of $X$ is $(\sum_k g_k^2)^{1/2}$. Gaussian
   183	  integration by parts gives $\E g^2 = 1$, $\E g^4 = 3$, and hence
   184	  \[
   185	    \E\|X\|_{S_4}^4=3n+n(n-1)=n(n+2)=288.
   186	  \]
   187	  Here $V_{\rm out} = n$ and $V_{\rm in} = I_n$. Keeping only the input variance
   188	  in~\eqref{E:finite-gaussian-maximum} would give fourth power
   189	  $9\operatorname{Tr}I_n^2 = 144$, which is false. Transposing the family
   190	  refutes the corresponding output-only bound. The average and maximum bounds
   191	  have fourth powers $1224$ and $2304$, respectively. This finite example
   192	  asserts nothing about a specialized wave estimate.
   193	\end{remark}
     1	\section{Frequency estimates and both wave variance directions}
     2	\label{S:wave-variance}
     3	
     4	We now apply the covariance and temporal estimates of
     5	Section~\ref{S:masked-covariance} to the full wave phase. We retain
     6	Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, write $a = \alpha_0$, and choose and fix
     7	\begin{equation}\label{E:variance-gamma-range}
     8	  0 < \gamma < \min\left(\frac12,\frac{2-\alpha}{2}\right).
     9	\end{equation}
    10	The interval is nonempty because $\alpha+a < 2$. We use $\langle\xi\rangle =
    11	\sqrt{1+|\xi|^2}$ and set
    12	\begin{equation}\label{E:variance-scale-profile}
    13	  B_\alpha(h) =
    14	  \begin{cases}
    15	    1, & \alpha < 1,\\
    16	    1+\log(1/h), & \alpha = 1,\\
    17	    h^{1-\alpha}, & \alpha > 1,
    18	  \end{cases}
    19	  \qquad 0 < h \le 1.
    20	\end{equation}
    21	
    22	\subsection{A scalar row estimate for a measure}
    23	
    24	Let $\nu$ be a positive Radon measure satisfying
    25	\begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-translated-growth}
    26	  \nu(B(y,r)) \le C r^\alpha,
    27	  \qquad y \in \R^d,\quad r > 0,
    28	\end{equation}
    29	where $C \ge 0$. If the estimate is initially known for open balls, apply it at
    30	radius $r+\epsilon$ and let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ to obtain the closed-ball
    31	estimate. Neither evenness nor a density is assumed here.
    32	Using~\eqref{E:masked-frequency-pair}, define
    33	\begin{align}
    34	  \Phi_h(\xi,\eta)
    35	  &:= \frac{\mathcal{Q}_h(|\xi|,|\eta|)}
    36	  {\langle\xi\rangle\langle\eta\rangle},
    37	  \label{E:frequency-row-kernel}\\
    38	  J_h(\xi)
    39	  &:= \langle\xi\rangle^{2\gamma}
    40	  \int_{\R^d}\Phi_h(\xi,\xi-\lambda)\nu(\ud\lambda).
    41	  \label{E:frequency-row-integral}
    42	\end{align}
    43	These are initially nonnegative extended integrals. In particular, the notation
    44	denotes a pushforward of $\nu$, not integration against an assumed spectral
    45	density.
    46	
    47	\begin{proposition}[Uniform scalar row]\label{P:frequency-row}
    48	  There is a finite $K = K(\alpha,a,\gamma)$, independent of $d,\nu,C,h$ and
    49	  $\xi$, such that
    50	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-row-bound}
    51	    \sup_{\xi\in\R^d}J_h(\xi) \le K C B_\alpha(h),
    52	    \qquad 0 < h \le 1.
    53	  \end{equation}
    54	\end{proposition}
    55	
    56	\begin{proof}
    57	  If $C = 0$, a countable covering by finite balls gives $\nu = 0$, and the
    58	  result is immediate. Suppose $C > 0$. For each $\xi$, let $\nu_\xi$ be the
    59	  pushforward under $\lambda \mapsto \eta = \xi-\lambda$. Then $\nu_\xi(B(0,R))
    60	  \le CR^\alpha$. For $q \ge 1$, put
    61	  \[
    62	    A_\xi(q) = \int_{|\eta|\le5q}\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}
    63	    \nu_\xi(\ud\eta).
    64	  \]
    65	  Choose $N = \lceil\log_2(5q)\rceil$, so $5q \le 2^N < 10q$. Splitting into the
    66	  unit ball and the annuli $2^j < |\eta| \le 2^{j+1}$ gives
    67	  \[
    68	    A_\xi(q) \le C\left(1+2^\alpha
    69	    \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}2^{j(\alpha-1)}\right).
    70	  \]
    71	  The geometric sum is bounded when $\alpha < 1$, is $N$ when $\alpha = 1$, and
    72	  is at most $2^{N(\alpha-1)}/(2^{\alpha-1}-1)$ when $\alpha > 1$. Hence,
    73	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-inverse-bessel}
    74	    A_\xi(q) \le K_\alpha C
    75	    \begin{cases}
    76	      1, & \alpha < 1,\\
    77	      1+\log q, & \alpha = 1,\\
    78	      q^{\alpha-1}, & \alpha > 1,
    79	    \end{cases}
    80	  \end{equation}
    81	  with a constant depending only on $\alpha$.
    82	
    83	  Set $q = \max(1,|\xi|)$ and $\epsilon = 1-2\gamma > 0$. On $|\lambda| \le 4q$
    84	  we have $|\eta| \le 5q$. Both bracket powers in $\mathcal{Q}_h$ are at most
    85	  one, since $a-1 < 0$. The contribution of this region to $J_h(\xi)$ is at most
    86	  \[
    87	    2\langle\xi\rangle^{-\epsilon}A_\xi(q)
    88	    \le 2q^{-\epsilon}A_\xi(q).
    89	  \]
    90	  If $\alpha < 1$, this is uniformly bounded
    91	  by~\eqref{E:frequency-inverse-bessel}. If $\alpha = 1$, the bound follows from
    92	  \[
    93	    e^{-\epsilon u}(1+u) \le 1+\frac1{e\epsilon},
    94	    \qquad u = \log q \ge 0,
    95	  \]
    96	  since $u e^{-\epsilon u}$ has maximum $1/(e\epsilon)$. If $\alpha > 1$, the
    97	  remaining power is $q^{\alpha+2\gamma-2}$, whose exponent is negative
    98	  by~\eqref{E:variance-gamma-range}. Thus, the near contribution is at most a
    99	  constant times $C$ in all three cases.
   100	
   101	  On the far region write $r = |\lambda| > 4q$. Then
   102	  \[
   103	    |\eta| \ge \frac{3r}4,\qquad
   104	    \big||\eta|-|\xi|\big| \ge \frac r2,\qquad
   105	    |\eta|+|\xi| \ge \frac r2.
   106	  \]
   107	  Each oscillatory bracket is at least $\langle hr\rangle/2$, whereas
   108	  $\langle\eta\rangle^{-1} \le 4/(3r)$ and $\langle\xi\rangle^{-\epsilon} \le
   109	  1$. Consequently, the far contribution is at most
   110	  \[
   111	    \frac43\,2^{2-a}\int_{|\lambda|>4q}
   112	    |\lambda|^{-1}\langle h|\lambda|\rangle^{a-1}\nu(\ud\lambda).
   113	  \]
   114	  Enlarge the domain to $|\lambda| > 1$ and split it into dyadic annuli.
   115	  Applying~\eqref{E:frequency-translated-growth} to their masses bounds this
   116	  expression by a constant depending only on $\alpha,a$ times $C S(h)$, where
   117	  \[
   118	    S(h) = \sum_{j=0}^\infty
   119	    2^{j(\alpha-1)}\langle h2^j\rangle^{a-1}.
   120	  \]
   121	  Choose $L = \lfloor\log_2(1/h)\rfloor \ge 0$. For $j \le L$ the bracket power
   122	  is at most one. For $j \ge L+1$ it is at most $(h2^j)^{a-1}$. Since
   123	  $\alpha+a-2 < 0$, the tail is
   124	  \[
   125	    \frac{h^{a-1}2^{(L+1)(\alpha+a-2)}}{1-2^{\alpha+a-2}}
   126	    \le \frac{h^{1-\alpha}}{1-2^{\alpha+a-2}}.
   127	  \]
   128	  The inequality uses $2^{L+1} > 1/h$ and the negative exponent. The finite sum
   129	  is bounded by $1/(1-2^{\alpha-1})$ for $\alpha < 1$, by $1+\log_2(1/h)$ for
   130	  $\alpha = 1$, and by
   131	  \[
   132	    \frac{2^{\alpha-1}h^{1-\alpha}}{2^{\alpha-1}-1}
   133	  \]
   134	  for $\alpha > 1$. Since $h^{1-\alpha} \le 1$ in the first case, we obtain
   135	  $S(h) \le K_{\alpha,a}B_\alpha(h)$. Combining the near and far bounds, and
   136	  using $B_\alpha(h) \ge 1$, proves the assertion and finiteness of the original
   137	  integral. All constants arose from numerical shell estimates and are
   138	  independent of $d$. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:frequency-row}.
   139	\end{proof}
   140	
   141	\begin{corollary}[A time exponent above one half]\label{C:frequency-time}
   142	  For every
   143	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variance-beta-range}
   144	    \frac12 < \beta < \min\left(1-\frac a2,
   145	    \frac{3-a-\alpha}{2}\right),
   146	  \end{equation}
   147	  there is a finite $K_\beta = K_\beta(\alpha,a,\gamma,\beta)$ such that
   148	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-time-bound}
   149	    h^{2-a}\sup_\xi J_h(\xi) \le K_\beta C h^{2\beta},
   150	    \qquad 0 < h \le 1.
   151	  \end{equation}
   152	\end{corollary}
   153	
   154	\begin{proof}
   155	  Both upper endpoints in~\eqref{E:variance-beta-range} exceed one half, by $a <
   156	  1$ and $\alpha+a < 2$. If $\alpha < 1$, use $2-a > 2\beta$ in
   157	  Proposition~\ref{P:frequency-row}. If $\alpha > 1$, use $3-a-\alpha > 2\beta$.
   158	  For $\alpha = 1$, set $\delta = 2-a-2\beta > 0$ and $u = \log(1/h)$. Then
   159	  \[
   160	    h^\delta(1+\log(1/h))
   161	    = e^{-\delta u}(1+u) \le 1+\frac1{e\delta}.
   162	  \]
   163	  This absorbs the critical logarithm. No endpoint value of $\beta$ is used.
   164	  This proves Corollary~\ref{C:frequency-time}.
   165	\end{proof}

1	\section{Covariance bounds for physically masked wave fields}
     2	\label{S:masked-covariance}
     3	
     4	We establish the covariance estimates needed for the operator construction.
     5	Throughout this section, Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} holds, $a = \alpha_0$, and
     6	$\Gamma \ne 0$. For zero spatial covariance, the spatial spectral measures and
     7	noise variances vanish; the purely temporal estimates remain valid independently
     8	of $\Gamma$. We use the unitary Fourier transform
     9	\[
    10	  \widehat{f}(\xi) = c_d\int_{\R^d}e^{-i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\ud x,
    11	  \qquad c_d = (2\pi)^{-d/2}.
    12	\]
    13	The spectral convention in Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} means that, for every
    14	complex Schwartz test $\varphi$,
    15	\begin{equation}\label{E:masked-spectral-convention}
    16	  \int_{\R^d}\varphi(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
    17	  = \int_{\R^d}\left(\int_{\R^d}e^{i\xi\cdot x}
    18	  \varphi(x)\ud x\right)\mu(\ud\xi).
    19	\end{equation}
    20	This is an identity of distribution pairings. We will not interchange two
    21	infinite measures in the associated oscillatory expression.
    22	
    23	A positive tempered Radon measure has polynomial mass growth. Indeed, choose a
    24	nonnegative compact smooth test that is at least one on the unit ball, and apply
    25	a defining Schwartz seminorm bound for the distribution to its dilations. Its
    26	mass on a ball of radius $R \ge 1$ is bounded by a power of $R$. Summation over
    27	dyadic shells then gives integrability of $(1+|x|)^{-N}$ for some $N$, and hence
    28	absolute integrability of every Schwartz test. These facts apply to both
    29	$\Gamma$ and $\mu$. Smooth cutoffs converge in the Schwartz topology, so these
    30	integrals agree with the tempered pairings.
    31	
    32	\subsection{Translated spectral growth and physical masks}
    33	
    34	\begin{proposition}[Translated spectral mass]\label{P:masked-spectral-growth}
    35	  Put
    36	  \[
    37	    M_\Gamma = \int_{\R^d}e^{-|x|^2/4}\Gamma(\ud x),
    38	    \qquad C_\Gamma = \frac{eM_\Gamma}{(2\sqrt{\pi})^d}.
    39	  \]
    40	  Then $0 < M_\Gamma < \infty$, and for $y \in \R^d$ and $r > 0$,
    41	  \begin{align}
    42	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
    43	    &= \left(\frac{r}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^d
    44	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{-iy\cdot x}\Gamma(\ud x),
    45	    \label{E:masked-gaussian-transform}\\
    46	    0 \le \int_{\R^d}e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
    47	    &\le \frac{r^\alpha M_\Gamma}{(2\sqrt{\pi})^d},
    48	    \qquad \mu(B(y,r)) \le C_\Gamma r^\alpha.
    49	    \label{E:masked-translated-ball}
    50	  \end{align}
    51	  The ball may be open or closed.
    52	\end{proposition}
    53	
    54	\begin{proof}
    55	  Temperedness gives finiteness of $M_\Gamma$. Its positivity follows from
    56	  $\Gamma \ne 0$. To check the Fourier constant, set $J(b) = \int_\R
    57	  e^{-Ax^2}e^{ibx}\ud x$ for $A > 0$. Squaring the real Gaussian integral and
    58	  using polar coordinates gives $J(0) = \sqrt{\pi/A}$. Differentiation and
    59	  integration by parts give $J'(b) = -bJ(b)/(2A)$. Therefore, $J(b) =
    60	  \sqrt{\pi/A}e^{-b^2/(4A)}$. Taking products over the coordinates gives
    61	  \[
    62	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{i(\xi-y)\cdot x}\ud x
    63	    = \left(\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}}r\right)^d e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}.
    64	  \]
    65	  Apply~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to the single Schwartz test
    66	  $e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{-iy\cdot x}$ to obtain \eqref{E:masked-gaussian-transform}.
    67	  Its left side is nonnegative. Taking the absolute value on the right removes
    68	  the complex phase because $\Gamma$ is nonnegative. The pushforward of $\Gamma$
    69	  by $x \mapsto rx$ assigns mass $r^{\alpha-d}\Gamma(A)$ to a Borel set $A$.
    70	  Thus,
    71	  \[
    72	    \int e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}\Gamma(\ud x) = r^{\alpha-d}M_\Gamma.
    73	  \]
    74	  This proves the Gaussian bound. On either ball $B(y,r)$ the integrand
    75	  $e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}$ is at least $e^{-1}$, proving the mass bound. This proves
    76	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-spectral-growth}.
    77	\end{proof}
   141	\begin{lemma}[Temporal covariance completion]\label{L:masked-time-completion}
   142	  Let $T > 0$. The form
   143	  \[
   144	    \langle f,g\rangle_a
   145	    = \int_0^T\int_0^T f(t)g(s)|t-s|^{-a}\ud t\ud s
   146	  \]
   147	  is positive semidefinite on real compact smooth tests. Its null-quotient
   148	  completion $H_a$ is separable. The inclusion of tests extends continuously
   149	  from $L^2(0,T)$, with
   150	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-time-schur}
   151	    \|f\|_a^2 \le \frac{2T^{1-a}}{1-a}\|f\|_2^2.
   152	  \end{equation}
   153	  In its complexification the norm is given by the same double integral with
   154	  $f(t)\overline{f(s)}$. In particular, bounded measurable amplitudes on a
   155	  subinterval, extended by zero, belong to this completion.
   156	\end{lemma}
   157	
   158	\begin{proof}
   159	  Write $\Gamma_E$ for Euler's Gamma function. Away from the null diagonal,
   160	  \[
   161	    |t-s|^{-a} = \frac1{\Gamma_E(a)}\int_0^\infty
   162	    \lambda^{a-1}e^{-\lambda|t-s|}\ud\lambda.
   163	  \]
   164	  This follows by substitution in the defining Gamma integral. Moreover,
   165	  \[
   166	    e^{-\lambda|t-s|}
   167	    = \int_{-\infty}^{\min(t,s)}2\lambda
   168	    e^{-\lambda(t-u)}e^{-\lambda(s-u)}\ud u.
   169	  \]
   170	  For each $\lambda > 0$ its quadratic form is an integral of a square. All
   171	  exchanges for compact smooth tests are absolutely integrable because the
   172	  kernel row integral is at most $2T^{1-a}/(1-a)$. The same bound and $2|xy| \le
   173	  |x|^2+|y|^2$ prove~\eqref{E:masked-time-schur}. A countable $L^2$-dense family
   174	  of compact smooth tests is consequently dense in $H_a$, proving separability.
   175	  The complex quadratic form is the sum of those of the real and imaginary
   176	  parts, since symmetry cancels the imaginary cross term. Thus, the same bound
   177	  holds after complexification. Smooth density in $L^2$, together with the Schur
   178	  bound on the absolute bilinear form, extends the inclusion and the integral
   179	  identity to $L^2$. This includes the stated interval amplitudes. This proves
   180	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion}.
   296	Write $\langle x\rangle = \sqrt{1+x^2}$. Let $I = [s,s+h] \subset [0,T]$, with
   297	$0 < h \le 1$. Norms below are those of the complexified temporal completion in
   298	Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion}.
   299	
   300	\begin{lemma}[Modulated amplitudes]\label{L:masked-temporal-modulation}
   301	  Let $A \in C^1(I;\mathbb{C})$, $M = \sup_I|A|$ and $D = \sup_I|A'|$. For every
   302	  real $\omega$,
   303	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-temporal-modulation}
   304	    \|1_IA(t)e^{i\omega t}\|_a^2
   305	    \le C_0(a)h^{2-a}(M+hD)^2\langle h\omega\rangle^{a-1},
   306	    \qquad C_0(a) = \frac{16}{1-a}.
   307	  \end{equation}
   308	  The bound is uniform in $T,s,h,A$ and $\omega$.
   309	\end{lemma}
   310	
   311	\begin{proof}
   312	  Put $c(v) = \int_s^{s+h-v}A(u+v)\overline{A(u)}\ud u$ for $0 \le v \le h$.
   313	  Differentiation at the moving endpoint gives
   314	  \[
   315	    c'(v) = -A(s+h)\overline{A(s+h-v)}
   316	    +\int_s^{s+h-v}A'(u+v)\overline{A(u)}\ud u.
   317	  \]
   318	  Thus, $c(h) = 0$, $|c(v)| \le hM^2$ and $|c'(v)| \le M^2+hMD$. Splitting the
   319	  covariance square into its two conjugate triangles gives
   320	  \[
   321	    \|1_IA(t)e^{i\omega t}\|_a^2
   322	    = 2\operatorname{Re}\int_0^h v^{-a}e^{i\omega v}c(v)\ud v
   323	    = 2h^{2-a}\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1 y^{-a}e^{i\omega hy}f(y)\ud y,
   324	  \]
   325	  where $f(y) = c(hy)/h$. Set $K = M+hD$. Then $f(1) = 0$ and $|f|,|f'| \le
   326	  K^2$. If $K = 0$ the assertion is immediate. If $|\omega h| \le 1$, the last
   327	  integral is at most $K^2/(1-a)$ in absolute value, and $\langle\omega
   328	  h\rangle^{a-1} \ge 2^{(a-1)/2}$. The claimed constant is sufficient in this
   329	  case.
   330	
   331	  Now suppose $k = |\omega h| > 1$. On $[0,1/k]$ the integral is at most
   332	  $K^2k^{a-1}/(1-a)$. On $[1/k,1]$, integrate the exponential by parts. The
   333	  endpoint at one vanishes, while the other endpoint contributes at most
   334	  $K^2k^{a-1}$. The derivative integral, divided by $k$, is bounded by
   335	  \[
   336	    \frac{K^2}k\left(a\int_{1/k}^1 y^{-a-1}\ud y
   337	    +\int_{1/k}^1 y^{-a}\ud y\right)
   338	    \le K^2 k^{a-1}\left(1+\frac1{1-a}\right).
   339	  \]
   340	  Here $k^{-1} \le k^{a-1}$ since $a > 0$. The total is at most
   341	  $4K^2k^{a-1}/(1-a)$. Finally, $k^{a-1} \le \sqrt{2}\langle\omega
   342	  h\rangle^{a-1}$ and $8\sqrt{2} \le 16$. Including the factor $2h^{2-a}$ proves
   343	  the bound for either sign of $\omega$. This proves
   344	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-temporal-modulation}.
   345	\end{proof}
   775	\section{Recovering the quadratic-exponential bound}
   776

    33	\begin{proposition}[Ground states and a uniform rate gap]

   216	for $(t,x) \in \R_+\times\R^d$, $d \in \{1,2,3\}$, interpreted in the
   217	Stratonovich sense (limit of classical wave equations driven by smoothed noises
   218	$\W_{\epsilon,\delta}$). The noise is centered Gaussian with
   219	\begin{equation}\label{E:cov}
   220	  \operatorname{Cov}\big(\W(s,x),\W(t,y)\big)=|s-t|^{-\alpha_0}\gamma(x-y),
   221	  \qquad 0<\alpha_0<1,
   222	\end{equation}
   223	where $\gamma \ge 0$ is nonnegative definite with spectral measure $\mu$.
   224	
   225	\begin{hypothesis}[Homogeneous covariance]\label{H:homog}
   226	  Let $d \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $0 < \alpha_0 < 1$. The spatial covariance is a
   227	  nonnegative, even, positive-definite tempered Radon measure $\Gamma$ on
   228	  $\R^d$, with positive even tempered Radon spectral measure $\mu$ in the
   229	  convention
   230	  \[
   231	    \Gamma=\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}\mu(\ud\xi)
   232	    \quad\text{in the sense of tempered distributions}.
   233	  \]
   234	  The symbol $\gamma$ in~\eqref{E:cov} denotes this covariance as a function
   235	  when one exists, and as a distribution otherwise. For every Borel set $A$ and
   236	  $c > 0$, $\Gamma(cA) = c^{d-\alpha}\Gamma(A)$, and
   237	  \begin{equation}\label{E:threshold}
   238	    \alpha_0+\alpha<2,
   239	  \end{equation}
   240	  with $0 < \alpha < d$, or $\alpha = d = 1$. In particular, the last case
   241	  includes spatial white noise $\Gamma = \delta_0$.
   242	\end{hypothesis}
   243	
   244	\paragraph{Zero covariance.}
   245	Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} allows $\Gamma = 0$ by design. In this case the
   246	centered Gaussian noise is $\W = 0$, and the solution with initial data
   247	$(1,0)$ is $u(t,x) = 1$. Thus $\E|u(t,x)|^p = 1$ for every $p > 0$, and
   248	all normalized logarithmic moment rates are zero. Results asserting strict
   249	positivity of covariance-dependent quantities impose $\Gamma \ne 0$ locally.
   250	
   251	Throughout we write
   252	\begin{equation}\label{E:kappa}
   253	  \kappa:=\frac{4-\alpha-\alpha_0}{3-\alpha}\in(1,2).
   254	\end{equation}
   255	
   256	\paragraph{Contribution of the present work.}
   257	We address the second moment of the original Stratonovich solution with
   258	fractional temporal covariance throughout Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}. The
   259	independent upper bound reaches the scale $t^\kappa$, rather than only the
   260	coarse quadratic exponential scale in the source. The main identification gives
   261	an intrinsic variational expression for the limiting constant over all
   262	nonnegative smooth compact spacetime controls, without a separability
   263	restriction. It retains the covariance amplitude, kinetic coefficient one and a
   264	Gaussian cost equal to one half of the variance, and includes the zero
   265	covariance case. The upper and lower comparisons refer to the same canonical
   266	solution. The occupation and spatial-energy estimates then give bounds on this
   267	constant; evaluating the white spatial energy is not a numerical evaluation of
   268	the full moment supremum. The earlier results discussed below concern different
   269	stochastic interpretations or temporal covariances and do not supply this
   270	identification by substitution.
